What this check cannot see

Read this first. These are outside what the check compares, so a difference there is not listed as a place.

  1. Pages without usable text. Pages without a usable text layer: scans, handwriting, pages whose only text is hidden OCR, and fonts whose characters have no names. They are listed as not checkable. Handwriting drawn on a typed page. White text on a white background: it is read as visible text.
  2. Order and structure inside an equation. Swapped letters inside an equation: symbols are compared as counts, not in order, so most swaps are not seen (the README gives the measured share). A superscript written as a subscript, or the reverse. A missing exponent group (which symbols a power covers). Two numbers of an equation that trade places (x² + 3 against x³ + 2): each number's digits and decimal point are compared, not where the number sits.
  3. Signs and symbols this check does not compare. Multiplication style (×, · or nothing). a/b written against a fraction bar. Brackets and fences. Accents other than arrows (hats, bars, dots, tildes), and an arrow over a letter where the PDF's text does not record it. A minus sign touching an arrow in a TeX-made PDF (x ← −1, a long arrow, an arrow over letters): TeX draws arrows from minus signs, so that minus may be part of the arrow and is not counted. Other symbols: dots and ellipses, stars and daggers (∗, †), ∴ and ∵, and any symbol the PDF prints as a glyph with no name (old Symbol fonts). A maps-to arrow (↦) counts as an arrow (→).
  4. Letter style the PDF's text does not record. Letter style (bold, double-struck, script) where the PDF's text does not record it. Bold letters in the prose, outside equations, where this check is unsure: a capital that starts a sentence or a paragraph, a label or list marker (also one set in the line, as in “Problem 1 a.” or options on one line), a letter in a bold word, line or heading, a letter whose sentence your HTML words differently or whose paragraph is not paired, and bold the PDF's font does not mark. Bold in your HTML is read from its markup and its own styles, never rendered. Small capitals: a font that prints small letters for capitals is read as small letters, so a letter-case place there may be the font, not the HTML.
  5. Maths not found or not paired. Maths the layout step does not find as an equation: maths in the body font, Chromium Type3 maths fonts, and display lines that include words. It is compared as text only. A whole PDF equation that your HTML leaves out is listed under Other differences, with a row in decisions.csv, not as a place to look at (correct equations are often not paired); with --exam, a display equation inside a question is a place to look at. Maths your HTML adds in a block of its own, outside a sentence, is counted (HTML maths not checked) but is not a place to look at, except with --exam, where it is one (outside table cells).
  6. Images and descriptions. Images, figures, alt text and figure descriptions: counted, not judged. Alt text on maths written in words: only its numbers and signs are compared, never its letters or what the words describe.
  7. Tables. Table structure (rows, columns, header cells). Cell text is compared as text only. In an ordinary HTML table, words that the PDF prints in another order (a label set across two rows, two header words that trade cells) are not listed; numbers and signs that trade cells are. A table whose rows the PDF's layout reads as one equation (numbers or maths in its cells, often a table typed without rules) is compared with your HTML's table as counts of its numbers, signs and words, not cell by cell: a number moved to another cell, or two numbers that trade places, is not seen. Each such table is counted, with a row in decisions.csv.
  8. How the maths is read aloud. How a screen reader or braille display reads the maths. TeX was read with latex2mathml, not MathJax.
  9. What a wording change means. Questions without a printed number are compared only as wording (their lettered options still as options). Options set side by side, in columns, as images or in tables are not compared as options, and one option set apart in bold or ticked is not looked for. Whether a change of wording changes the meaning. Every change is shown; none is judged.
  10. Whether the PDF is right. Whether the PDF itself is correct. A mistake in the PDF passes through, and a correction in the HTML shows up as a difference.
  11. Presentation and delivery. Visual presentation, content hidden by CSS or loaded by scripts, and delivery through a learning management system (only static notes are given).
  12. Other accessibility needs. Other accessibility needs. Use axe and a person.
